newsitem.title: FRANCE: French trucker talks advance but strike goes on.
newsitem.headline: French trucker talks advance but strike goes on.

text.p: Striking truckers reported progress on Wednesday in marathon negotiations but vowed to tighten their stranglehold on the French economy to make employers do more to end the nationwide protest now in its 10th day.

The giant Force Ouvriere union said that "significant progress" had been made toward a deal on retirement at 55 instead of 60, one of three key points of contention in the most serious labour unrest to hit France this year.
They said agreement on that point would permit the talks to move on to the truckers' remaining demands for shorter hours and higher pay.
But they said they would not consider any issue definitively settled until agreement was reached on all points.

"The possibility of retiring at 55 after 25 years of service, at 75 percent of pay, constitutes a base which enables us to seriously contemplate pursuing the discussions," the FO said in a printed statement.
But the union went on to denounce the employers' "intransigence" on the remaining issues of pay and hours.

"At this stage of the negotiations and given the stakes, the employers' proposal to raise salaries by one percent is viewed as a provocation," the statement said, encouraging truckers at blockades across the country to step up their protests.
The truckers have mounted nearly 200 barricades on roads and around refineries and petrol depots across France in a protest that has started to cut deeply into economic activity.

Some factories were forced to close their doors because they could not obtain raw materials while farmers reported spot shortages in animal feed as grain shipments were prevented from reaching feed processors.

Wednesday was also a test of wider union disaffection in France. The big Communist-led CGT union has urged workers to rally at the barricades to express support and step up pressure on Prime Minister Alain Juppe to drop austerity policies.
Pilots, stewards and engineers at French airlines mounted a parallel two-day strike early in the day, forcing state airline Air France to cut back on its flight schedule.
A spokesman said Air France planned to provide two-thirds of long-haul and just a quarter of medium-haul flights due to the union protest over feared job cuts and restructurings.

The airline's short-haul unit Air France Europe, which operates mainly domestic routes, expected to cut more than half its flights. It said it would guarantee 213 flights on Wednesday and 200 on Thursday, against 480 normally each day.
On the railways, three unions were staging a 24-hour strike from Tuesday evening at the Sotteville-les-Rouen depot in northwest France, a symbolic bastion during last year's strikes.

The barricades around refineries and fuel depots were forcing the closure of some petrol stations, and petrol rationing has been imposed in some parts of the country so that supplies could be maintained for fire engines and ambulances.
The strike was also starting to disrupt mail, grain imports and angering foreign truckers blocked on French roads.

The French franc stayed under pressure as traders said markets feared the strike could spread, or that the government would agree to the strikers' demands and encourage costly copycat strikes in other sectors.
